THE UNIVERSITY Appendix B OF RHODE ISLAND Revised 8/2016 Notice of Change form Notice of Change for: M.S. in Healthcare Management; Post-Baccalaureate Certificate in Health Leadership and Administration; and Post-Baccalaureate Certificate in Quality Improvement, Process Measurement, and Information Systems Management Date: October 20, 2020 A. PROGRAM INFORMATION 1. Name of institution University of Rhode Island 2. Name of department, division, school or college Department: n/a College: College of Business 3. After several rounds of discussions between the healthcare management program director (Sean Edmund Rogers) and URI Online leadership, as well as analysis of current and prospective student data, we wish to make the following changes to streamline URI’s healthcare management offerings and to enhance their marketability: 1. Ask #1: Offer a single healthcare management graduate certificate instead of the two separate certificates that currently exist, and allow a wider selection of healthcare management (MHM) courses to count towards that single certificate.

2.
Ask #2: Change the composition of the M.S. degree such that it straightforwardly requires the completion of 30 credits of MHM credits.
Currently, the M.S. degree is structured as the combination of (1) one 12-credit post-baccalaureate certificate, (2) a second post-bac certificate, (3) one MHM elective, and (4) a practicum capstone.
This totals 10 MHM classes and 30 MHM credits.
The certificate portion of this is a so-called stackable certificate approach, with 24 of the 30 credits coming from these two post-bac certificates.
Our desire is to streamline the M.S. in Healthcare Management degree such that it is comprised of 30 MHM credits whether or not a student completes a graduate certificate en passant.
Our primary objective with this entire change proposal is #1 above – to make earning a graduate certificate in healthcare management at URI more accessible.
Per URI Online recruiters and prospectors, there has not been a single expression of interest in the post- bac certificate in quality improvement.

Students are certainly interested in quality improvement and this is an important topic in healthcare; however, none have expressed a desire to devote an entire program of study to this subject.
Any interest in earning a healthcare grad certificate at URI has been directed toward the other existing certificate in health administration.
Additionally, prospective students have expressed strong interest in being able to earn a certificate by taking courses outside of the strict structure that currently exists (at present, three of the four courses in each certificate are prescribed).
The current structure limits when students can begin and complete a certificate – they must wait until the carousel of courses comes back around for them to hop on, and in some cases that can be a year-long wait.
Creating a single certificate in healthcare management enables URI to alleviate these pain points and reach a wider audience of prospective students.
We have found that most prospective students interested in a grad certificate wish to begin quickly, and URI Online has the structure in place to enable that to happen.
The limiting factor is our current program design.

A side effect of creating a single graduate certificate in healthcare management is that the “stackable certificate” design of the M.S. would need to go away and be replaced with a straightforward 30-credit MHM approach.
There is no evidence that removing the notion of stackable certificates would do harm.
No prospects in recent memory have expressed interest in earning the stackable certificates as a pathway to the M.S. degree.
In fact, it has created confusion during prospect calls and sessions. 2

As a final sidenote on the topic of stackable certificates, in my professional opinion (as a scholar of human resources) such a design may even adversely impact URI’s ability to provide accessible healthcare management graduate education to Rhode Islanders and beyond.
As I learned this summer via meetings with enrollment services, financial aid, and URI Online, our healthcare management graduate certificates do not qualify for federal financial aid.
Some graduate certificate programs around the country do qualify for federal aid, but our healthcare management ones were determined not to.
Thus, students must pay for all certificate credits (up to 24 under the current “stackable” model) with non- federal financial aid, such as out of pocket or via private loans.
At current rates, that amounts to $18,792 for two URI certificates.
This has led to more than one prospective student not applying or enrolling at URI this summer and fall.
The streamlining we propose potentially removes barriers to access and may help put URI graduate education within reach for more aspiring healthcare professionals and leaders.

Summary: In sum, the newly-proposed M.S. degree structure would include all the same courses as before.
We are not changing the curricular offering at all - we are simply proposing that the stackable certificate design be removed.
That’s ask #2 above.
And we are asking for it to be removed because we wish to offer a single grad certificate in healthcare management that offers flexibility and frequency for learners (instead of two separate certificates that are narrowly tailored).
That’s ask #1 above. 6.

But there does seem to be opacity around the administrative apparatus.

It remains unclear how those numbers factor in as KPIs under the budget model, so the move could still have a budgetary impact even though the direct course revenue path is well-defined.
FSEC will need to monitor in an ongoing way and be mindful of any other administrative changes that are proposed, as they could have similar unpredictable consequences. 4.
Continued Items 4.1 Faculty Concerns submitted through the FS Webpage - No new concerns. 5.
Updates 5.1 Updates (meetings with administrators, other committee meetings) i.
APC review - Textbook and course materials policy - reviewers requested - Pres.
Williams explained that the use of the campus bookstore as a comprehensive course materials outlet is absolutely essential.

It does not have to be the only avenue available to students but does need to be an option.
Although there have been well-known delays and complications in the bookstore securing 3

materials, the alternatives pursued by faculty in lieu of the bookstore can easily become a logistical and ethical minefield.
Concerns were expressed that the current bookstore retailer has attempted to force faculty to standardize course materials across all sections of a given course and this is a serious infringement of faculty rights.
The FS Pres. and VP met earlier with the Student Senate President who voiced a concern that textbook affordability has become a serious issue for undergraduates.
Federal mandates around student aid use make bookstore cooperation even more important.
That being said, the APC is about to update its Textbook and Course Materials Policy and has asked the FSEC officers and other volunteers to serve as reviewers; Sens.
Daniels and Trimm volunteered.
Policy readers are asked to review the draft carefully and provide margin notes or other comments and concerns for APC staff. ii.
PSC meeting of 1/27/26 - The meeting included a report about the university's transition away from Ecampus HR to WorkDay (the State as a whole has already transitioned).

If all goes well, the university may consider transitioning to WorkDay’s student module in the future. iii. ‘Survey Design Advising Team’ - JVW Sen.
Van Wyk consented to launch and manage this service for the foreseeable future.
Pres.
Williams noted he needs to present the idea to the Provost’s office for a reaction before the initiative goes to the senate, possibly for a March introduction.
The senate office is happy to host the resource and forms on their webpage with links to the Provost’s pages, if desired. iv.
Senate appointments to Library Dean search - Pres.
Williams has completed the appointment of two faculty members. v.
Copyright statement - No report ; still under review by the General Counsel. vi.
Commencement schedule - FSEC assignments - TBD following election of a new VP/President-elect (on 2/29), who should be given the opportunity to choose the extent of their role. vii.
Chapter 2 UM amendments - Status of revisions - for February adoption?
There were some related concerns about the decision to split the position of the Vice Provost for Academic Personnel and Budget in two.

Some edits to the draft are in progress and it is hoped that the senate is still on track to accept the changes in February. 6.
Report of the Coordinator i.
Student worker hiring update - The FS office is on-boarding two graduate student workers who are starting right away. ii.
Senate elections and February VP election - Staff is waiting for the current full-time faculty list from the Provost’s team which is required to prepare apportionment notices.
The office is also designing an electronic ballot for the VP election, which will run differently this year than in years past due to new UM updates. iii.
Parliamentarian - The FS Parliamentarian serves at the pleasure of the FS President and this individual does not need to be a senator to serve.
If the current Parliamentarian continues past his term expiration, FSEC should consider providing compensation.
FSEC members agreed unanimously. iv.
New question - What prevents a faculty member from teaching in another department?
This question was raised to staff from a sitting senator who offered the example of an Engineering faculty member being qualified to teach calculus or physics from inside the engineering department.

FSEC members explained that course codes belong to department heads;additionally, per the AAUP contract, chairs are responsible for assigning teaching responsibilities. 7.
New Business – Open for additional items not listed in the agenda. 4

i. Changes to qualifications for emeritus status - Some concerns have been transmitted to the Provost’s office and FSEC is waiting for a reply. ii. Brightspace purge - Faculty are complaining about the loss of resources but FSEC members agreed the 5-year horizon is more than reasonable and faculty members have the option of archiving materials themselves. It is not expected that the university will have Brightspace ‘forever’ and FSEC members queried if there is a plan in place for archiving or recovering materials after Brightspace is offboarded. Pres. Williams will assign the CTI the task of gleaning more information. iii. multiple paid resources for communications (CTI issue) - Tabled to next week’s meeting. 8. Closing Remarks – Recap of decisions made, action items, and plans for the next meeting. A question was asked about the recent Snow Day, wherein faculty were prevented from offering any remote synchronous options. Pres. Williams noted that decision was the result of the university’s Weather and Other Emergencies Policy wherein that stipulation is clear. Asynchronous options are not affected. 9. Adjournment - The meeting adjourned at 2:34 pm. 5

Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee Report # 2020-2021-2 to the Faculty Senate Faculty Senate Meeting February 18, 2021 Proposal to Change Faculty Senate Committee Structure The following recommended changes update the University Manual language passed by the Faculty Senate referring to the recently revised Faculty Senate committee structure (FS Bill # 20-21-14).
Recommended Changes: Motion: accept changes to the University Manual on committee structure language changes in 5.78.12, 5.84.13, 8.20.14, 8.20.17, 8.20.30, 8.70.10, 8.70.12, 8.70.13, 8.70.20, 8.70.61, 8.70.72, 8.81.50, 8.81.80 Changes: 5.78.12 Membership.
The committee shall comprise the Director of the Office for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning who shall serve as Chair, and the Assistant Director of Online Learning and the Director of Media & Technology Services by virtue of their positions.
The Provost shall appoint a designee from the Office of the Provost, and a dean of a degree-granting college.
The Faculty Senate shall appoint six faculty members to staggered three-year terms.

A graduate student and an undergraduate student, appointed respectively by the Graduate Student Association and the Student Senate, shall also serve on the committee.
The faculty appointees shall represent the University Libraries, the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the General Education Committee Subcommittee, and the Graduate Council and may represent more than one of these constituencies.
Faculty appointees may succeed themselves once. #12-13–1 #15-16-15D #16-17-21, #17-18-23 5.84.13 The membership shall include faculty members appointed by the Faculty Senate: two from Arts & Sciences, one from each of the other degree-granting colleges and one from the University Libraries, one faculty representative of each of the following committees: the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the General Education Committee Subcommittee, the Teaching, Advising, and Assessment Committee, and the Graduate Council.
Faculty representatives should be individuals involved in assessment in their departments/colleges.
All faculty appointments shall be for three-year staggered terms.

In addition, administrative members shall include the Vice Provost for Faculty Affairs; the Dean of University College for Academic Success or the dean’s designee; the dean of a degree-granting college; one designee of the Vice

President for Student Affairs; one representative of the Office of Institutional Research; the Director of the Office for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning or designee; and the Assistant Director of the Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment, and Accreditation.
A graduate student and an undergraduate student, appointed respectively by the Graduate Student Association and the Student Senate, and a student representing the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies, shall also serve on the committee.
A faculty member appointed by the Faculty Senate in consultation with the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs shall chair the committee. #06-07–25, #07-08–40 #14-15–31 #15-16-15D #16-17-21, #17-18-23 8.20.14 Any course that assesses two (2) of the General Education Student Learning Outcomes may be submitted to the Curriculum and Standards General Education Committee for approval to fulfill General Education requirements, regardless of that course’s place in a major or prerequisites.

No college, department, major, minor, or other program or course of study may require a student to choose a specific course to satisfy the General Education requirements, although courses that fulfill requirements or prerequisites for majors which also happen to satisfy General Education requirements can be recommended through advising.
Of the courses taken to complete General Education requirements, only up to 12 credits may share the same disciplinary code.
An exception to the limit is allowed for the HPR (Honors Program topic) course code.
Only courses that fulfill the D1 Student Learning Outcome, Integrate and Apply, may be graded using S/U.

Of D1 courses graded S/U, a student may apply only up to 6 credits to the total 40 credits needed to complete the General Education requirements. #13-14-21, #15-16-13 #16-17-26B, #17-18-23 8.20.17 The General Education Committee Subcommittee shall, through the using course review standards calibrated to those in use by the Curriculum and Standards Committee, make recommendations to the Faculty Senate regarding implementation and administration of General Education and shall report periodically its evaluation of the General Education Program, including a review of the appropriateness of courses for General Education. #13-14-21, #15-16-13, #17-18-23 8.20.30 Director of General Education.
A Director of General Education, selected from the University faculty, shall coordinate and advocate for the General Education Program.
The Director shall, in concert with the General Education Committee Subcommittee, be responsible for the overall management of the General Education Program.
The Director shall report to the President of the Faculty Senate, keeping the Faculty Senate Executive Committee informed of current issues as requested.
Questions of jurisdiction regarding joint responsibility for the General Education

Program shall be referred to the Faculty Senate.
The Director shall be released from one half of his/her normal duties and shall be compensated for work done during summers.
Normal duties shall include, but not be restricted to, teaching, assigned research, advisement, committee work and thesis direction. #16-17-31, #17-18-23 8.70.10 Preparation.
A six-year calendar for fall, winter, and spring semesters shall be maintained.
In accordance with sections 8.70.20-8.70.61, the Office of Enrollment Services each fall shall prepare a new sixth-year calendar and submit it to the Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee by the end of October.
The Committee Subcommittee shall review the calendar and present it to the Curriculum and Standards Committee on time so that the calendar can be presented to the Faculty Senate by December 1. #01-02-27, #02-03–32, #12-13-21, #16-17-23, #17-18-23, #18-19-34 8.70.12 Unless acting in response to the declaration by the Senate Executive Committee of an emergency situation as stated in By-Laws 4.28, the Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee, adjustments to a proposed calendar may not be made on the floor of the Senate.

Instead, a proposed calendar, along with instructions about possible revisions, must be referred back to the Academic Calendar Committee, which Subcommittee.
The Curriculum and Standards Committee shall resubmit the calendar at the next Senate meeting. #01-02-27, #16-17-23, #17-18-23 8.70.13 Recommendations regarding rescheduling class days missed within an academic year as the result of natural calamity, work stoppage, etc. shall be the responsibility of the Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee, whose proposal shall be subject to the approval of the Curriculum and Standards Committee and subsequent approval by the Faculty Senate or, under circumstances requiring expeditious implementation, subject to the approval of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee only after a public hearing on the action scheduled with at least a 48 hour notice. #05-06–1 #14-15-32, #16- 17-23, #17-18-23 8.70.20 The Academic Year.
The beginning and ending dates of each semester shall be the same for all colleges and schools of the University.

Exceptions may be granted to the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies and to fully-online accelerated programs (which will run on the fully-online accelerated calendar).
Requests for exceptions shall be received by the Curriculum and Standards Committee on time such that they can be transmitted to the Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee no later than October 1 of the preceding academic year. #14-15–08, #16-17-23, #17-18-23

8.70.61 A six-year calendar for the Summer Session shall be maintained.
The Office of Enrollment Services, in consultation with the Assistant Director of Summer Session and Winter J-Term, each fall shall prepare a new sixth-year calendar and submit it to the Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee by the end of October.
The Committee Subcommittee shall review the calendar and present it to the Curriculum and Standards Committee on time so that the calendar can be presented to the Faculty Senate by December 1. #01-02-27 #16-17-16, #16-17-23, #17-18-23, #18-19-34 8.70.72 The two-year calendar for the fully-online accelerated program shall be developed by the Office of Online Education, in consultation with the Office of Enrollment Services, and submitted to the Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee by March 1 of the year preceding the one during which the calendar is to become effective.

The Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee shall review the calendar for the fully-online accelerated program and present it to the Curriculum and Standards Committee on time so that it can be presented to the Faculty Senate for approval by April 1 of the year preceding the one during which the calendar is to become effective. #14-15–08, #16-17-23, #17-18-23, #18-19-34 8.81.50 Scheduling Courses.
Courses submitted to the Office of Enrollment Services for scheduling shall be certified by the department chairperson via the academic dean as being permanently approved or authorized temporary courses.
A new course or course change proposal form must be processed through the college curriculum committee, Curriculum and Standards Committee or General Education Committee where appropriate, and/or Graduate Council, and approved by the Faculty Senate before being scheduled. #17-18-23 8.81.80 Course Jurisdiction.
The content, textbook, over-all conduct and method of presentation of single section courses shall be the responsibility of the instructor.
The administration of multi-section courses shall be determined by departments.

Modifications that significantly change a course (e.g. lecture to online offering, lecture and lab to lecture) require approval through the proper curricular channels (e.g. college curriculum committees) to the Curriculum and Standards Committee or General Education Committee when appropriate, and/or the Graduate Council, and the Faculty Senate. #06-07-33, #17-18-23

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) We propose an undergraduate interdisciplinary minor in Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities.
The United Nations defines social justice in terms of human rights and personal dignity for everyone.
Other sources include access and equality.
Borrowing from these descriptions, we define social justice broadly as the value of human life, equal access to social capital, personal dignity, and the implementation of human rights for ALL.
US Citizenship and Immigration Services identifies core civic responsibilities that include staying informed about issues affecting your community and participating in them.
More importantly they add respecting the rights, beliefs, and opinions of others, and participating in the democratic process.
We adopt these descriptions of civic responsibilities for the minor.
Course options for the minor represent an array of multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary approaches to social justice topics.
Students who complete the
3 minor will emerge with a nuanced understanding of the world around them, the

4 reasons why people continue to seek to change that world, and a familiarity with the organizing tools and strategies available to those efforts.
A core intellectual component of the minor is an emphasis on seeing the world through the lens of other people's experiences, especially people and groups who have different social, racial, ethnic, economic, religious, gendered, and geographic backgrounds from one's own.
Developing a critical consciousness of the intersections of one's identities, privileges, and power is another important component.
This can lead to more compassionate and meaningful relationships with others.
Moreover, a deep understanding of one's positionality can help perpetuate or dismantle systems and structures that ultimately impact minoritized communities.
Students will learn about subtle and blatant institutional barriers and the micro-aggressions that systematically oppress people.
Students will have experiential learning opportunities that allow them to see the ways in which the ideas they read about and discuss in class actually play out in the real world.

Students will engage in civic processes visiting with community leaders, activists, and politicians to influence policies.
They will prepare for and engage in civic processes reflecting on these experiences.
They will learn theories, methods, and skills that they can use in their work and personal lives to improve the human condition.
Courses for the minor are organized into three categories; peoples, social and institutional contexts, and methods and skills, and students are required to take at least one course from each category (and not more than three) and then complete their credit requirements in consultation with advisors.
An ongoing advisory committee of faculty, staff, and peers will meet once per semester to review advising strategies, and tweak the course offerings, making sure that courses are still being offered, that faculty who teach them are informed about the minor, and review new course options that become available to include in the minor.
The committee will also develop and distribute marketing materials for the minor and maintain a Google work site for students who pursue the minor and for faculty and staff who contribute to it.

This site will also serve to inform the community about experiential learning opportunities that arise in the interest of social justice and civic responsibilities.
Currently, the committee includes several faculty, staff, and undergraduate students.

RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable need for the program.
B1.
Why is the new program being developed?
The world is experiencing monumental institutional changes that have arisen from centuries of oppression against groups of people by age, gender, socioeconomic status, ability, sexual orientation, regionalism, religion, race, ethnicity and nationality.
As a species, we cannot tolerate or participate in group oppression any longer, but the institutionalized nature of systemic oppression requires that people must enter the work- force, build their families, and engage in their communities with the knowledge and skills necessary for creating change.
This is the responsibility of our educational system.

Regardless of a student's major course of study, every one of them should graduate being prepared to create positive change that improves the lives of everyone.
A minor in social justice and civic responsibilities, coupled with the student's major course of study provides a path toward creating positive change in the world.
B2.
What is the economic need and workforce data related to the program?
Students who complete the minor will explore their connections to the communities in which they live and work, tackling questions of mutual obligation, social and political change, and human impact on the social, historic, and geographic world.
Grounded in an interdisciplinary approach that includes the humanities, social sciences, the arts, and other fields - this new minor will provide students at URI with a foundation for a life of actively challenging systems of oppression. and decolonizing received wisdom, produced knowledge, and told histories [or public memory].
At the same time, students will gain the critical thinking, reading, writing, and analytical tools that are the foundation of an informed and educated citizenry.

Our students will enter the workforce with skills in human relations that every industry needs for a diverse world.
It is no longer sufficient to train a select few individuals to expertly advise organizations how to navigate diversity.
Everyone must learn the values of a diverse workforce to ensure that each individual can reach their/her/his best potential.
Regardless of a student's major academic and career interests, pursuing the minor in social justice and civic responsibilities will enrich their lives and bring these ideas and skills into all industries, organizations, and occupations.

6 a.
Provide information on jobs available as a result of successfully completing the certificate or degree: job titles, job outlook/growth, and salaries.
Since this is a minor and not a major course of study, it is intended to enrich the work and personal lives of everyone, not just those who are in a select few careers.
For example, a student majoring in criminology and criminal justice who pursues a career in policing would be more marketable in that career with a sub-specialty in social justice and civic responsibility, as would a nurse, a teacher, an engineer, or a psychologist, for example.
The skills and information learned in this minor are important for journalists, museum curators, researchers, professors, executive directors of non-profit and social justice organizations, politicians, diplomats, UN officials and advisors, community organizers, community educators (like people at Save the Bay, etc.), entrepreneurs including people piecing together careers through podcasting, and freelance writing.

According to the Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training (RIDLT), the top 10 occupations requiring a Bachelor's degree include registered nurses, elementary and secondary school teachers, and child, family & school social workers.
All of these occupations are projected to show increases in job openings through 2026, all of them require extensive work with the public, so this minor would make our graduates more marketable in these careers.
Organizational rules are changing to include more diverse and equitable processes and roles are being introduced to ensure these processes are followed.
Most people who currently occupy positions of power, in this particular moment, were not taught the skills that are necessary to achieve these goals.
They will be looking for people who have received the kind of education that specifically leads to social justice in any occupation.
A graduate with a minor in this area would be of interest to a company's corporate responsibility division, and human resources positions dedicated to talent diversification.
The RIDLT projects jobs under the Training and Development Specialists category will see a 12.2% increase in jobs by 2026.

INSTITUTIONAL ROLE: The program should be clearly related to the published role, scope, and mission of the institution and be compatible with other programs and activities of the institution.
C1.
Explain how the program is consistent with the published role, scope, and mission of the institution and how it is related to the institution's Academic Plan.
The University's mission explicitly highlights these values; "diversity, fairness, and respect," and "civic involvement." URI's "Academic Strategic Plan (2016-2021) sets as Goal 4, "diversity and social justice" that is defined to "Inspire an enlightened community that is characterized by vibrant cultural diversity; that embraces difference; that is built upon a learning environment that fosters respect, understanding, and social justice; and that rejects prejudice and intolerance." The first strategy under this goal is to diversify faculty and staff.
Often, members of the URI community who are from underrepresented groups feel disengaged and unwelcomed.
They may embrace inclusion in the advisory committee for this minor and they would greatly contribute to the committee's goals.
